newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: New docks keep Singapore ahead in ship repairs.
newsitem.headline: New docks keep Singapore ahead in ship repairs.

text.p: The recent opening of two new huge dry docks reaffirmed Singapore as an international ship repair centre, but the near-term fortunes of the island state's major yards remain difficult, marine analysts said.
The long-awaited recovery in ship repair remained elusive and new docks just added to the industry's major problem -- too many of them and not that many ships to repair, they said.

Combined ship repair profits of Singapore's three major yards -- Keppel Shipyard, Sembawang Corp and Jurong Shipyard -- have slumped to about Singapore $27 million (US$19 million) in the first half of the year and analysts say the second half is not expected to be much better.
In 1991 and 1992, ship repair profits for the three yards amounted to S$245 million.
The new docks by Keppel and Jurong, costing over Singapore $200 million, would boost repair capacity in the island state by by a third to three million dead weight tonnes (dwt).
"There is severe overcapacity in the industry worldwide. Even when the turnaround in ship repair comes, we won't see boom times like that of 1991," said analyst Koh Bee Ann with GK Goh Securities.
So Keppel and Jurong will have to wait several years before recouping their investments in their new docks.

"In the good old days, we would have recouped our investment in three years," Jurong chairman Lua Cheng Eng told reporters. Now, it would take seven to eight years to earn back the money spent on the new 400,000 dwt dock, he said.
Analysts said the new docks were started two to three years ago, when the companies expected a recovery by 1995 or 1996.

But it has not materialised and new yards in the Middle East and China, where labour costs are lower, have taken business from Singapore. The strong appreciation of the Singapore dollar in the past two years has also kept ships away.

"The local yards have now to compete in a much tougher international arena, against its more experienced Middle Eastern rivals and substantially cheaper (by 15-20 percent) Chinese yards," said HG Asia in its latest note on ship repair.
Singapore yards have responded by cutting prices.
"They are quite competitive now, but it also means their margins have been under pressure," said Sim Chey Hoon, an analyst with Merrill Lynch.
Analysts said they estimated profits had sunk to as low as five percent compared with 20 percent early in the decade.
Sim said she did not expect the outlook for the yards to get worse but that any recovery would be a mild one.
When that recovery might come about is still a big question.
Jurong managing director Tan Kwi Kin said it would be "very difficult to say if a recovery would be seen next year".
He said the tanker market was doing better, but "the improvements have not been able to encourage shipowners to undertake major surveys and repairs."

Keppel is more optimistic. At the launch of the group's 360,00 dwt drydock last week, group managing director Loh Wing Siew said he expected a recovery by next year as charter rates for tankers had risen strongly.
